circuit_splits.question: What counts as "notice of the entry" that opens the short window (7 days in the 1991-2005 text) to move to reopen the appeal time under FRAP 4(a)(6): only written notice from the clerk or a party, any written notice, or actual notice of any kind?
circuit_splits.rules: Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)(6) (1991 text, restyled Dec. 1, 1998); Fed. R. App. P. 26(a); Fed. R. Civ. P. 77(d)

sides.label: A: written notice from the clerk or a party required
B: any written notice received counts, whoever sends it, no Rule 77(d) mailing needed
C: actual notice (e.g. counsel viewing the docket) counts

circuit_splits.acknowledgement: Bass (5th Cir. 2000) surveys the disagreement expressly ("Some circuits have expressly held ... On the other hand, the Eighth and Ninth Circuits speak in terms of actual notice"). Wilkens (5th Cir. 2001) says "we disagree with the portion of the Benavides opinion" requiring notice from the court or a party. Benavides distinguishes the Eighth and Ninth Circuit positions. Outcome differs: the same facts (a lawyer learning of the order from someone other than the clerk or a party) open the window in B and C but not in A.
circuit_splits.outcome_sensitive_example: Benavides (oral report from a third-party lawyer) leaves the window shut and the motion timely; under Wilkens-style any-written-notice or Nunley-style actual-notice the clock would have run from the earlier contact.

circuit_splits.question: When did the one-year grace period for pre-AEDPA convictions (28 U.S.C. 2244(d), 2255) end: April 23, 1997 (one year counted without Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)) or April 24, 1997 (Rule 6(a): exclude the day of the event, last day is the anniversary)?
circuit_splits.rules: Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a) (pre-2009 text, applied to statutory periods); 28 U.S.C. 2244(d)(1)
circuit_splits.acknowledgement: Flanagan (5th Cir. 1998) surveys circuits that "simply announced that the reasonable time period will expire on April 23 or April 24" and notes the Second Circuit alone had addressed Rule 6(a). Hernandez (4th Cir. 2000) overrides the Fourth Circuit's own April 23 dicta (Brown v. Angelone and later cases) because the date was outcome-determinative. Patterson (9th Cir. 2001), footnote: "The only Circuits espousing the April 23, 1997 deadline are those that have not specifically addressed the applicability of Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)" (naming Calderon (Beeler), Burns, Goodman, Simmonds).
circuit_splits.caveat: The April 23 statements are dicta in cases where the date did not decide the result; the split is a split in announced rules, resolved by about 2001 in favour of April 24. The rulings on the April 24 side (Patterson, Hernandez, Flanagan) are outcome-determinative.
circuit_splits.outcome_sensitive_example: Patterson: petition filed 1998-06-19 is timely under the Rule 6(a) anniversary method; the district court had held it one day late. Hernandez: filed 1997-09-09, timely only under April 24.
circuit_splits.status: confirmed from the opinions themselves (with the dicta caveat)
